title: Peace three times: om shanti
hook: a student gives back all he learned, partridges peck it up, and their school asks for peace
carry: shanti three times: within, around, beyond
tomorrow: what did Krishna say about results you can't control?

segments.voice: Yesterday, bha and prana: the breath the body can't live without, riding out inside every holy word. Today, the peace that rides out on it.

The Vishnu Purana tells how one school got its strange name. A teacher, Vaishampayana, and his proud student, Yajnavalkya, fall out. The angry teacher says: then give back everything you learned from me. And Yajnavalkya does. He brings up the verses he had learned, right there. The other students take the form of partridges, tittiri, and peck them up. That, the story says, is why their branch of the Veda is called Taittiriya: the partridge school.
screen: `GIVE BACK WHAT YOU LEARNED.` → `PARTRIDGES PECK IT UP.` → `THE PARTRIDGE SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: Now hear the peace chant that opens the second part of the Taittiriya Upanishad, still chanted before study across India. Teacher and student say it together: may God protect us both, may God nourish us both, may we work together with strength, may our study shine, and may we not hate each other. Some teachers hear the story in that line: a school born of a quarrel between teacher and student asks, every time it begins, not to quarrel. Then comes om, shantih, shantih, shantih. Why three times? The traditional explanation is that suffering comes from three directions, so peace is asked three times. Adhyatmika: trouble from within, your own body and mind. Adhibhautika: trouble from other beings, the people and creatures around you. Adhidaivika: trouble from beyond anyone's control, storm and fate and the powers above. Peace within, peace around, peace from beyond. That's why so many Hindu prayers, pujas and readings close this way. And listen to how it ends. Shantih is written with a visarga, an h with a dot under it; in Devanagari, two small dots like a colon. It's a release of breath after the vowel, and reciters often let it carry a faint echo: shanti-hi. Some keep it faint, some let it ring. Om closes with the other mark, anusvara, a hum through the nose. So the chant ends the way it asks: the word is over, and the peace is still breathing out.
screen: `MAY GOD PROTECT US BOTH.` · `MAY WE NOT HATE EACH OTHER.` · `SHANTI: WITHIN, AROUND, BEYOND.` · `VISARGA: SHANTI-HI.` · then, large: `THE PEACE STILL BREATHING.`

segments.voice: If you chant, say om and let the m hum until the breath runs out. Then say shantih three times, slowly, one on each out-breath, letting the visarga carry its soft echo. With the first, think of your own body and mind; with the second, the people and creatures near you; with the third, everything no one controls. If you would rather not chant, say the word peace three times inwardly, with the same three in mind.
Visarga. The breath after the vowel, as in shantiḥ, said shanti-hi: the peace still breathing out.
Your line: shanti three times: within, around, beyond. One word, three directions. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Teachers and students across India chant saha nāvavatu before study, and countless pujas, readings and gatherings close with om shantih shantih shantih, traditionally explained as peace from three sources of trouble; reciters let the final visarga breathe out softly.

fork.reveal: may we not hate each other, then peace three times. some teachers hear the partridge school remembering its own quarrel.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: śāntiḥ, peace. The two dots at the end are the visarga.

trapdoor: what you thought: om shanti shanti shanti is one word said three times for effect.
what it means: the traditional reading asks peace from three directions: within, from others, and from what no one controls.
what a scholar hears: the three kinds of suffering (adhyatmika, adhibhautika, adhidaivika); the saha nāvavatu chant of Taittiriya 2.1 with mā vidviṣāvahai; the visarga closing śāntiḥ.

chat.meaning: The traditional explanation: suffering comes from within, from other beings, and from beyond anyone's control, so peace is asked three times. The Taittiriya chant before it asks teacher and student not to hate each other.

tie.story: Yajnavalkya quarreled with his teacher and gave back all he'd learned; the partridge school that came of it chants 'may we not hate each other' and then peace three times.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Sam each shanti asks peace from one side: within her, from the people around her, and from what no one controls.
tie.you: which of the three peaces do you need this week?

visarga.meaning: a breath released after a vowel, written as an h with a dot

anusvara.meaning: a hum after a vowel, carried through the nose

shantih.meaning: peace; said three times to close a chant

Yajnavalkya.meaning: the proud student who gave back what he learned

Taittiriya.meaning: the partridge school, a branch of the Yajur Veda

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1 (the opening peace chant, saha nāvavatu)

Taittiriya 1.1 (sham no mitrah sham varunah...) closes with om shantih shantih shantih; the summary 'asks for friendship from the gods and protection for teacher and student' is loose; confirm or reword.

Visarga echo (shanti-hi, nama-ha) is described as what reciters often do, with variation acknowledged; confirm. Anusvara described as a nasal hum; strictly it assimilates to the following consonant in many recitation styles. A Keeper may want a note.
saṃskṛta spelled with anusvara and vocalic ṛ: confirm. The meaning of the name is deliberately not given (claims rule on etymology).
Practice offers a wordless alternative for those who prefer not to chant om or shantih.
